text: Start at the Esmeralda Trailhead (end of North Fork Teanaway Road, ~4,243 ft) and follow the Ingalls Way Trail. At about 0.3 mile, stay right onto Ingalls Way where it leaves the Esmeralda Basin Trail; at about 1.7 miles (5,440 ft), turn right at the Longs Pass junction rather than continuing to Ingalls Basin, and switchback up open slopes to Longs Pass (roughly 3 mi, ~2,100 ft gain from the trailhead, cresting around 6,400 ft) — the pass gives the first clear look at Stuart's west aspect. From the pass, descend steep, sometimes dusty/scree-y trail on the north side, losing about 1,300 ft in a mile, to reach Ingalls Creek in the timber below. Cross the creek (a straightforward rock-hop or wade in normal summer flow, the last reliable water source before the ridge) and pick up the climber's path heading west, up-valley, toward Stuart Pass. Well short of the pass itself (roughly 6,200–6,400 ft), leave the trail and traverse climber's-left (north) across open talus and heather benches toward the base of the West Ridge — this cross-country traverse is where parties most commonly go astray, since there is no maintained tread and several minor gullies look similar; aim for the obvious deep gully (the middle of three parallel gullies) marked by a large, house-sized boulder at its base. An alternate, longer northern approach via the Stuart Lake Trailhead and Stuart Pass exists but adds significant mileage and is not the standard line. Plan on 3.5–5 hours car-to-base depending on route-finding and snow conditions; some parties camp near Ingalls Lake or in the upper Ingalls Creek basin to break the day up. Hazards: the Longs Pass descent and creek-crossing slopes hold snow into early summer and can be icy at dawn; the final talus traverse to the ridge is loose and exposed to rockfall from parties above; there is no water beyond the Ingalls Creek crossing, so tank up there for the long day ahead. Getting past Long John Tower and the exposed West Ridge Notch traverse are the route's main route-finding dilemmas; high on the route, below the summit, a short dihedral with a fixed piton (5.4) or a layback further along the ledge (5.6) leads to easier fifth-class climbing to the top.
runs: a short dihedral with a fixed piton 5.4 or a layback further

text: From the notch, climb easy Class 4 a short way, then step left around a blind corner onto the north side of the ridge. Exposure jumps sharply here with the Stuart Glacier far below. Protection is small to medium cams and nuts; a short rope is enough for the whole upper section. Belay where the terrain steepens left of the crest.
runs: left around a blind corner onto the north

text: From I-90 Exit 32 (436th Ave SE), turn north over the freeway and drive 0.5 mile to SE North Bend Way. Turn left, and in 0.25 mile turn right onto SE Mount Si Road. In 2.9 miles, past the Little Si and Mount Si trailheads, the paved Mount Teneriffe Trailhead lot is on the left. A Discover Pass is required to park.
runs: on the left a discover pass is required to park

text: Above the chimney, follow the long snow finger up the upper face, scramble the wildly exposed crest, and traverse around a small tower to the notch between the false and true summits. Take the false summit on an exposed easy fifth-class hand traverse, downclimb it, and make the short climb to the true summit.
runs: traverse around a small tower to the notch

text: Accounts of this West Ridge / Crescent Creek Basin descent range from three to five rappels, depending on how much of the gully a party downclimbs between stations - one describes two rappels to reach the top of the gully and three more in the gully itself. The anchors are existing tat and slings, including a large chockstone, so carry extra webbing and lockers to back up or replace what is there.
runs: rappels to reach the top of the gully and

text:
The start is just left of the snowfield at the bottom of the face, after the wall is accessed from its west side. From the Crescent Creek Basin camp the technical start is reached by crossing the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn col and descending the Mustard Glacier into McMillan Cirque, then rounding into position under Terror's wall. Cross the glacier remnant beneath the face, then start just left of the snowpatch at the bottom.

The moat where snow meets rock at the base is the usual obstacle, and it is also the marker: you are at the base when you are standing at the gap between the snowpatch and the wall, on its left.

The decision that defines this route, and it is made before the hard climbing rather than during it: the face is split by two ribs, and this route takes the right, or western, one. The main risk on the lower face is not difficulty but committing to the wrong rib. Long, mostly third-class pitches climb above the snowfield while traversing steadily rightward; the face is over 2,000 ft tall with limited options to reverse. If your traverse is taking you left, you are on the wrong half of the wall.

Two confirmations higher, both visual and both usable in thin cloud: aim for the right or western crest of the buttress about two thirds of the way up the lower face, identifiable by the rock darkening. And A sharp prow marks roughly the lower third of the buttress. Darkening rock and a sharp prow are features of this rib and not of its neighbour.

What the upper face gives you: a long snow finger forming a ramp that carries the route a good distance, then scrambling on a wildly exposed crest, a traverse around a small tower to the notch between the false and true summits, an exposed easy-fifth hand traverse over the false summit, a downclimb, and the short climb to the true 8,151 ft top.

On the approach, when crossing from Stump Hollow into Crescent Creek Basin: do not drop into the low notch north of the chopping block. The correct line into Crescent Creek Basin is about 100 yards north of that notch, at a flat, bivy-site shelf on the ridge.
runs: traverse around a small tower to the notch
the low notch north of the chopping block

text: The long snow finger on the upper face forms a ramp that carries the route for a good distance; carry what you need to climb it. Above its top, the climbing turns to scrambling on a wildly exposed ridge crest, then a traverse around a small tower to the notch between the false and true summits. The false summit is taken directly on an exposed easy fifth class hand traverse, then downclimbed before the short climb to the true 8,151 ft top. Rock quality deteriorates near the top, with steep, extremely loose ground reported; a fatal-consequence rockfall accident on this buttress involved a sizeable block that had appeared solid tearing loose. Descent is normally the West Ridge gully. This is one of the longest and most committing lines in the range and retreat from high on it is genuinely difficult.
runs: the long snow finger on the upper face
traverse around a small tower to the notch
is one of the longest and most committing

text: A more moderate day than the north-side routes: slabs lead directly from camp to the saddle between Terror and Degenhardt, then a short, steep 4-pitch ridge/face climbs straight to…
runs: to the saddle between terror and degenhardt then

text: A more moderate day than the north-side routes: slabs lead directly from camp to the saddle between Terror and Degenhardt, then a short, steep 4-pitch ridge/face climbs straight to the top, then descended by the West Ridge gully, with rappels, back into Crescent Creek Basin and camp.
runs: to the saddle between terror and degenhardt then

text: Widely regarded as the most inspiring line on Terror's north side: Stoddard traversed left of the 1961 route to gain a cleaner crest, following solid rock through a narrow face between two buttresses and a long, spectacular arete section to the summit area.
runs: traversed left of the 1961 route to gain

text: An exposed step out over the gully on the left, then a right-trending chimney feature up to trees; one easy 5.6 move off the ground, then low 5th to the tree belay.
runs: an exposed step out over the gully on the left

text: A short wall (watch for a stuck cam at the top) leads through dirty tree ledges and steps to a belay at the base of a hanging slab.
runs: dirty tree ledges and steps to a belay at the base of

text:
Aim for the lowest point in the ridge, and know in advance that it is further left than it looks. From Bumblebee Basin, scrambling up scree, the beginning of the ridge that you can see from below is not where you want to be. The notch you want is left of it, at the ridge's lowest point, around 5,960 ft. That single correction is the most useful thing on this approach, because the eye pulls you right every time.

The notch is small, and its size is the confirmation: it holds about three people at most. If you have topped out on a broad, comfortable saddle, you are not at the start of the West Ridge.

Expect short fourth-class scrambling around gendarmes to reach it. Once you top out on the ridge you scramble over a small gendarme, traversing rightward toward the crest, to gain the notch itself.

The first move settles it absolutely: pitch one begins with a step left into a well-featured chimney. That step-left-into-a-chimney is the signature of this route and is probably the crux of the whole climb. If your first pitch is a face or a slab, you are not in the right notch. The first two leads run up a series of chimneys in solid rock.

And the other route on this peak is on the opposite side: the East Ridge is class 3-4 and is gained from a notch at about 5,600 ft on the ESE side, from the same basin. If you are on easy scrambling ground the whole way, you are on the East Ridge and you have circled to the wrong end of the mountain.
runs: up a series of chimneys in solid rock

text: P1 climbs an open book on climber's left to a ledge, then a second short open book; P3 traverses right to a gully with a large detached-block belay anchor; P4 starts up a mossy gully past a rusty piton before angling left through cleaner rock.
runs: gully with a large detached block belay anchor

text: Three options exist, and the choice depends on party speed and whether you're continuing to Forbidden Peak. (1) Reverse the South Ridge: downclimb interspersed with numerous short, traversing rappels off fixed slings/anchors that are 'in abundance' along the ridge — a single rope is generally sufficient for these short raps, but carry extra webbing/cord to back up or replace tat, since stations are alpine-style (slung horns, chockstones, occasional old fixed gear) rather than bolted. This option is slower but avoids the moat problems of the SE Face line. (2) Descend the Southeast Face: downclimb from the summit area to the top rappel station, then make 5-6 double-rope (60m) rappels down the SE Face gully/slab system back toward the Taboo Glacier — the second station is on climber's left, the rest are straight down or climber's right. The crux of this option is the final rappel, where you must cross a moat/bergschrund to reach the snowfield below; this can be genuinely difficult and its condition can't be scoped from above, so the first person down should carry a picket, ice axe, and crampons to help climb out of the moat if needed. Bring two ropes (or a single rope doubled) for these double-rope rappels. (3) Continue over the summit and descend via the Torment-Forbidden Traverse toward Forbidden Peak (sustained exposure, a 5.6 step and ~45-degree snow/ice) if that's the day's objective — this is a full traverse, not a simple descent, and commits you to exiting via Forbidden's West Ridge/Boston Basin instead of returning the way you came.
runs: should carry a picket ice axe and crampons to

text: From SR 20 at Marblemount, follow Cascade River Road about 22.5 miles to the small Boston Basin pullout, passing the Eldorado parking area at about mile 20. The first 10 miles are paved and the rest is rough gravel.
runs: the first 10 miles are paved and the rest is

text:
From the unsigned Boston Basin pullout on Cascade River Road at roughly 3,300 ft (about 21.7 miles from Marblemount, directly opposite Johannesburg), take the old Diamond Mine roadbed about three quarters of a mile to a mile, then the sharp right turn onto the steep climbers' trail. Four small creek crossings, treeline about 5,300 ft, low camp 5,300-5,500 ft, high camp about 6,200-6,400 ft.

From high camp leave any semblance of trail and make a rising traverse to the northwest, holding roughly the 6,200 ft contour across talus, tundra and slab steps. You pass beneath the south spur of Forbidden Peak and cross a prominent rock rib below the cliffs, with the Taboo Glacier coming into view above.

Gain the Taboo Glacier on its climber's-left side and follow it up. Some parties skip the summit-day traverse entirely by carrying up the Taboo and camping at about 7,100 ft directly beneath Torment's southeast face at the foot of the couloir.

This traverse is the part that gets people lost in cloud. It is open, uniform ground with no trail, and in early season the creek channels are buried and there is avalanche exposure across it.
runs: pass beneath the south spur of forbidden peak and

text: Follow the old mining road about three quarters of a mile to the old mine site, then take the sharp right onto the steep, unmaintained climbers' trail. It switchbacks up through forest with four creek crossings to treeline around 5,300 ft, then eases across heather benches and talus into Boston Basin, with high camp at roughly 6,200 to 6,400 ft.
runs: of a mile to the old mine site

text: From US 101 about 0.9 mile south of the Quilcene Ranger Station, bear right onto Penny Creek Road. In about 1.5 miles take the left fork onto Forest Road 27 and follow it about 12 miles, then turn left onto Forest Road 190 and follow it about a mile to its end at the upper trailhead, a small gravel lot at about 3,300 ft. No parking pass is required.
runs: 1.5 miles take the left fork onto forest road 27 and follow it

text: The poorly protected pitch (often called PG13): traverse down and right around the first gendarme on an exposed ramp on the right side of the ridge, over mossy, lichen-covered and sometimes wet slabs and turf. Protection is marginal and rope drag builds quickly; extend placements.
runs: traverse down and right around the first gendarme
exposed ramp on the right side of the ridge

text: One of eleven summits in The Needles, a range of jagged Eocene sandstone-and-pillow-basalt spires that radiate north from Mount Deception and form the west wall of Royal Basin in the dry, rain-shadowed eastern Olympics. Walkinshaw (7,378') is the range's northernmost and most accessible peak — first climbed in 1961 by Joe Munson and Jim Parolini — sitting just north of higher, harder Mount Clark (7,528') and range-highpoint Mount Johnson (7,680'). The group lies within the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness of Olympic National Park, draining to Royal Creek on the east and the Gray Wolf River on the west.
runs: the west wall of royal basin in the

text: From the T-intersection at the end of North Lake Cushman Road, turn right onto FS Road 24 and continue about 1.5 miles, then turn left onto FS Road 2419 and follow it up the Big Creek drainage for roughly 6.6 miles to its end at a small trailhead and parking area near 3,026 ft. Display a Northwest Forest Pass; no wilderness permit is needed.
runs: 2419 and follow it up the big creek drainage

text: From the T-intersection at the end of North Lake Cushman Road, continue right onto FS Road 24 for about 1.5 miles, then turn left onto FS Road 2419 and follow it up the Big Creek drainage for roughly 6.6 miles to its end at a small trailhead/parking area at about 3,026 ft. From here the 'trail' quickly becomes a boot path and then largely off-trail scrambling — there is no numbered maintained trail for most of the route. The path climbs directly and steeply through forest for the first stretch, hand-over-hand on roots and rock in places, gaining several hundred feet before breaking out of the trees into a couple of open meadow benches (the most reliable early-season water, via lingering snowmelt seeps, is generally found in this meadow band — by mid-to-late summer expect it to be dry, so carry all the water you'll need from the car). Above the meadows the route enters scree and talus slopes and stays primarily on the climber's-left side of a large, loose rocky gully; this section is tight in spots with a lot of unconsolidated rock, so groups should stay spread out (not stacked directly above/below each other) to avoid raining rocks on people below. In spring and early summer this gully can hold avalanche-prone snow and may require an ice axe. The path winds above the gully until it gains Mount Washington's southern ridgeline, then follows a faint, exposed climbers'/goat trail along the ridge crest — in multiple spots the tread narrows to barely one boot-width with real exposure on both sides (this is the section referred to as the 'Dog Walk Ledge'); solid class 3 with a couple of class 3+/4 moves, and not a place for hesitant scramblers. The ridge trail leads to a scree field below the false summit (greasy and slick if wet) and a 'goat trail' up its climbers'-right edge to a stone wind shelter on the ridge, from which a final short class 3–4 scramble gains the true 6,255 ft summit.
runs: 2419 and follow it up the big creek drainage

text:
From the T-intersection at the end of North Lake Cushman Road, go right onto FS Road 24 for about 1.5 miles, then left onto FS Road 2419 and follow it up the Big Creek drainage roughly 6.6 miles to its end at a small trailhead at about 3,026 ft. Northwest Forest Pass to park; no wilderness permit is needed.

From here the trail quickly becomes a boot path and then largely off-trail scrambling — there is no numbered maintained trail for most of the route. It climbs directly and steeply through forest, hand-over-hand on roots and rock in places, to a couple of open meadow benches around 3,800 ft. That meadow band holds the most reliable early-season water via snowmelt seeps; by mid-to-late summer expect it dry, so carry what you need from the car.
runs: 2419 and follow it up the big creek drainage

text: Park at the Watson Lakes Trailhead at the end of FS Road 1107 (elev. ~4,300 ft), reached via Baker Lake Road (FS-11) south around Baker Lake on FS-1106 and out FS-1107 to road's end. From the trailhead, follow the Anderson-Watson Lakes Trail #611 into the woods; at about 1 mile you'll pass the junction with the Anderson Butte Trail #611.1 (stay straight/right for Watson Lakes). Around 1.5-2 miles, at roughly 4,700 ft, a second junction splits: right drops 0.5 mile to lower Anderson Lake, while the left fork climbs 0.5 mile to a small saddle entering the Noisy-Diobsud Wilderness before dropping to the Watson Lakes (4,400 ft) near 2.5-3 miles in. The lakes are notoriously buggy in summer and are the last reliable water — treat before filling up, since there's no dependable source higher on the mountain. From Watson Lakes the maintained trail ends and the route becomes an open, cairned/boot-path climbers' route: leave the basin and climb talus (and snow well into summer) on Watson's north/west slopes toward the ridge crest. The standard and easiest line follows the widest gully east of the peak up to a saddle at about 5,900 ft on the ridge; a western gully alternative has a dangerous moat and rotten snow bridge late-season and should be avoided. From the 5,900-ft saddle, traverse along the ridge and across a steep slope to wrap around the base of the summit block. A short, loose class 2-3 dirt-and-rock gully (10-15 ft) gains the true summit ridge, which is a narrow (~30 ft), exposed class 2-3 catwalk with real drop-off on both sides — a hand line is commonly carried and recommended for this final airy section. Total round trip runs roughly 7-9.5 miles with 2,500-3,000 ft gain depending on exact trailhead/camp and route-finding; parties camping partway (e.g., ~5,400 ft on the north slopes) shorten the summit day considerably. Route-finding above the lakes is the main approach hazard in poor visibility since the line is unmarked talus/snow rather than trail.
runs: across a steep slope to wrap around the base of the summit block a short

text: From the 5,900-ft saddle, traverse along the ridge and across a steep slope to wrap around the base of the summit block.
runs: across a steep slope to wrap around the base of the summit block

text: A hard-sided bear canister is required for food storage at every wilderness camp in the park, Elwha camps included — bear wires are not an approved method (free loaner canisters available at the Port Angeles Wilderness Information Center). The Elwha River and its tributaries are closed to fishing.
runs: the elwha river and its tributaries are closed to fishing

text: From the lot, walk up through the woods toward the wall on an unmaintained, intermittently cairned climbers' line, gaining elevation quickly, then traverse left through open forest and across slabby benches to a shoulder at the base of the wall's right-hand side. Allow an hour to an hour and a half.
runs: the base of the wall's right hand side
an hour to an hour and a half

text: Turn off the highway a little over four miles east of Washington Pass, following signs for the Cutthroat Creek trail, and drive about a mile to the trailhead lot, which has restrooms. Do not confuse this with the Cutthroat Peak approach, which starts from an unmarked highway pullout well west of here and serves a different objective entirely. Start on the maintained Cutthroat Creek Trail, then leave it a short way along and walk up through the woods toward the wall — the ground gains elevation quickly at first, then the line traverses leftward through open forest and across slabby benches. There is no maintained tread on this section; parties report cairns and an intermittent climbers' path, but treat it as open-forest navigation rather than a trail. The traverse ends on a shoulder at the base of the wall's right-hand side, which is where the climbing starts. Allow the better part of a couple of hours from the car to the base.
runs: miles east of washington pass following signs for the cutthroat creek trail
the base of the wall's right hand side

text: The shoulder at the right-hand end of the wall is the arrival point, and the route starts on low-angle ground, not steep ground. The traverse through the forest and across the slabby benches deposits you on a shoulder at the base of the wall's right-hand side; that shoulder, rather than any point along the middle of the cliff, is where you should be standing. From it, the start of this route is clean, low-angle crack systems running up a big ramp that trends left as it rises. Low angle and left-trending together are the test. This wall holds only two known lines and the other one is several grades harder and sustained, so if what is above you is steep, continuous crack climbing with no ramp under it, you have walked past the start and are beneath the hard line. Likewise, if you are still in trees and have not come out onto a distinct shoulder with the right edge of the wall above you, you have not finished the traverse. Expect the cracks on the lower pitches to be bushy and dirty rather than clean — that is normal here and is another sign you are on the right, less-travelled line. The upper pitches merge into the harder route's corner and finish on its final blocky pitch, and the descent rappels that line.
runs: the base of the wall's right hand side

text: The summit path is now more worn than the trail it leaves, and the wrong turn has a name. Navaho Pass is unmistakable ground — small, rocky, sparsely vegetated and wind-exposed, with the Stuart Range filling the view — and it is where the trail meets the old crest trail along the county line. Head east out of the pass, paralleling the range. The old boot-path junction that descriptions still mention has effectively vanished: the beaten track now is the summit path, more worn than the crest trail beside it, so the thing to look for is the most-used tread rather than a faint branch. If instead you follow the connecting ridge left from the pass, you are heading for Wrong Turn Peak, which is what it is called and why. Two more confusions worth knowing: the prominent peak straight ahead on the walk in is Little Navaho, not this one, and the final ridge throws up several false tops before the true summit, which is small — barely higher than a rocky outcrop just east of it. On the way down, do not follow the southeast ridge all the way toward Little Navaho; there are cliffs below it.
runs: head east out of the pass paralleling the

text: The longest and most continuous narrow snow gully on the left side of Tiffany's north face, averaging 40 degrees with steeper sections to 55 degrees.
runs: most continuous narrow snow gully on the left side of

text: From Winthrop, take the East Chewuch River Road north about 6.5 miles and, before it crosses the Chewuch River, turn right onto FR 37. Follow FR 37 about 13 miles, turn left onto FR 39 and drive about 7.5 miles, past Freezeout Pass, to Tiffany Springs Campground at about 6,760 ft. FR 37 from Conconully reaches the same junction. The gravel is rough, closed to trailers and usually snowbound until late June. Northwest Forest Pass required.
runs: the chewuch river turn right onto fr 37

text: Take Trail #373 from across the road past Tiffany Lake and up to Honeymoon Pass at about 7,150 ft (about 45 minutes). Leave the trail and traverse south along the grassy east slope below the crest into the small cirque under the north face at about 7,360 ft, then climb the longest, most continuous snow gully on the left side of the face to the summit ridge and the summit.
runs: snow gully on the left side of the

text: From Tiffany Springs Campground (6,760 ft), hike trail #373 east past Tiffany Lake to Honeymoon Pass (7,150 ft, ~45 min). From the pass, traverse SW/south along the east slope below the ridge crest to the small cirque at the base of the North Face (7,360 ft), then continue to the base of the couloir. Driving access: via Conconully/North Fork Salmon Creek (~21 mi, ~1 hr, rough road, 4WD recommended), via the South Fork/Baldy Pass (~30.6 mi, ~2 hr, 2WD gravel), or via the Methow Valley (~26.5 mi, ~1 hr, 2WD gravel).
runs: along the east slope below the ridge crest to the small cirque at the base of the

text: From SR 20 in Winthrop, take the West Chewuch Road (County Road 1213) about 6 miles to where it joins FR 51, then follow FR 51 up the Chewuch valley about 22 miles to the end of the pavement and turn right into the Andrews Creek Trailhead at about 3,050 ft. Fill out the free self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit at the trailhead; a Northwest Forest Pass is needed to park.
runs: a northwest forest pass is needed to park

text: A light rack of nuts and several long slings suffices for the brief 5.3 sections.
runs: light rack of nuts and several long slings

text: Gain the ridge by scrambling up the grassy southeast slope from the Boundary Trail, then follow the long, broken crest that runs from The Pope toward Cathedral's summit. Each pitch is mostly scrambling with a move or two of 5.3, graded old-school, so expect it to feel stiffer than the number. A light rack of nuts and several long slings for horns is enough.
runs: light rack of nuts and several long slings

text:
You are aiming for the long broken ridge that runs between Cathedral Peak and The Pope, a separate small peak further north along the same crest, sitting right on the Canada–United States border.

That relationship is the base-finding and it is also the warning. The ridge has a peak at each end. If you keep working north along the crest past the point where the ground starts descending away from Cathedral, you are heading for The Pope and, shortly after that, for an international border it is illegal to cross here.

The route itself confirms as you go rather than at a single spot: each pitch has a move or two of old-school 5.3 with scrambling between, so seven pitches of mostly-easy ground with occasional short difficulties is correct here and is not a sign you have wandered onto the walk-up. The real crux announces itself — about 400 feet below the summit you cross a dike, and the two short pitches immediately above that dike are the hardest climbing on the route. A final airy fourth-class scramble finishes it.

Negative marker for the start: if you find yourself entering a deep gully with a detached tower on your right, you have walked to the SE Buttress start. The NE Ridge is gained from open grassy slope off the main trail, with no gully involved.

Descent is the ordinary walk-up route to the west, and a short rappel may be wanted to get off the summit ridge.
runs: each pitch has a move or two of old school 5.3

text: From Needle Peak, follow the connecting ridge south over the North and South Anonymity Towers (low fifth class), climb the Dark Glacier to Dark Peak, then follow the high, wild crest to Bonanza's west summit and run the knife-edge ridge to the main summit; the last two pitches hold the hardest climbing, at 5.8.
runs: the knife edge ridge to the main summit

text:
From the notch, downclimb about 200 vertical feet and traverse to the first obvious gully. That is the published test and it is the one that works in cloud, because it is counted rather than seen: you are not identifying a gully by its shape from a distance, you are walking beneath the face from a fixed point and taking the first one you meet.

Why that matters here more than anywhere else on this page: this face carries five closely spaced ice and mixed lines — Pineapple Express, Blue Moon, New York Gully Direct, New York Gully and LA Express — and they are near enough together that racking up under the wrong one is the normal failure. Count from the notch, do not pick by appearance.

The pitch-one confirmation, and it is a good one: ascend roughly 200 ft up the gully and then take an obvious ramp out to the left, belaying from a quasi-cave. Gully, then a left-trending ramp, then a cave belay. If your first rope length does not offer a left ramp at about 200 ft, you are in a neighbouring line.

The second confirmation is higher and unambiguous: the route runs up obvious weaknesses to a small headwall split by a 5.8 crack, historically aided and now freed. That crack is the route's signature. A line with no headwall crack is not New York Gully.

And a honest warning about the approach itself: most of it is through thick timber and the published advice is to go with somebody who knows it or follow an existing skin track. Without a track, expect it to be slow and to be the part of the day where you lose time.
runs: 200 vertical feet and traverse to the first obvious gully

text:
Two established ways off the summit; both are widely used and either works, but they return you to different spots relative to a gear stash at the base.

Bolted West Face rappel line (most direct back to packs at the base of NW Corner/West Face): from the summit, downclimb/walk skier's-left to the top of a clean, purpose-bolted rappel line down the right side of the West Face. Six bolted (2-bolt) rappel stations in a nearly direct line bring you back down to essentially the same spot where you left your pack at the base of the route. Pulls are reported as clean and the line is efficient — regulars find it a breeze. A single 60m rope is just barely sufficient (one station, reportedly the 3rd rappel, is tight enough that you may need to reach down to clip your PAS/daisy to the anchor and feed rope through your device to reach it); a 70m rope removes that squeeze and is the more comfortable choice. No natural anchors needed on this line — it's fully bolted.

Classic notch/chockstone descent (South/Southwest Gully): downclimb and rappel the south side into the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire, then continue down the Southwest Gully (the South Early Winter Spire "Chockstone Route" descent). This runs three single-rope rappels from near the summit down to the notch/gully (which often holds snow even in summer), followed by one spectacular, largely free-hanging double-rope rappel down and past a huge chockstone (~50 ft of air), then a final short rappel (~30 ft, off a tree anchor) or downclimb/scramble to reach the base. Total is about 4-5 rappels on this line. Anchors are natural/fixed slings around the chockstone and trees rather than bolts — inspect webbing before trusting it. Summit-to-base time on this descent is typically around 1.5-2 hours. This option is the standard descent if you climbed a route on the south/southwest side, or as a backup if the West Face bolt line is congested or iced.
runs: into the notch between north and south early

text: Loose fourth-class climbing continues along the exposed arête crest with a dramatic drop to the glacier below.
runs: with a dramatic drop to the glacier below

text:
The bergschrund at roughly 6,500 ft is the base, and the couloir above it is the only one. Beckey and Schmidtke's own account of the first ascent puts them at the bergschrund at the foot of the final north face at 6,500 ft, with 800 ft of 50-degree ice couloir above. That is the arrival: a schrund, then a single steep couloir that guards the Tower.

The ridge between the two glaciers is the handrail. From the Price Lake moraine you climb a rib with the Price Glacier on one side and the East Nooksack on the other. In cloud you do not need the Tower: keep a glacier on each side of you and go up. If you only have ice on one side, you have come off the rib.

The saddle is the hinge, and it is counterintuitive. From the bivy the traverse is climber's right to an exposed snow saddle below the Tower, and then you drop down onto the main lobe of the Price Glacier. Losing height here feels wrong and is correct. A party that refuses to descend off the saddle stays high on the wrong side and never reaches the couloir.

Confirm at the schrund: the couloir starts around 50 degrees and steepens to about 60 at the top, with a single 70-degree step where it hits rock. If your line eases off rather than steepens, it is not the couloir. Parties have found the schrund hollow and swung wide left to avoid it entirely — that is a known variation, not a sign you are lost.

What going too far looks like: continuing up the Price Glacier past the Tower's couloir puts you on the Price Glacier route on Shuksan, which is a different mountain's climb reached from the same basin. Nooksack Tower is the freestanding tower below and north of Shuksan's summit; if the ground above your couloir keeps going for thousands of feet rather than ending on a tower in about 1,200 ft of fourth class, you are on Shuksan.
runs: the bergschrund at the foot of the final

text: The South Face is the steeper 'back side' of the tower located directly above the East Nooksack Glacier, presenting as much vertical relief as the north aspect but steeper. The route starts on the right side of the south face with front-pointing up a short couloir before transitioning to rock climbing. Pitches angle slightly left and upward, passing a short overhanging bulge and entering a large depression. Simulclimbing leads up and left out of the depression to the left-center portion of the south face and eventually the summit.
runs: as much vertical relief as the north aspect
on the right side of the south face
depression to the left center portion of the south face

text: Descend by downclimbing and rappelling the standard north face route on the front (north) side of the tower rather than retracing the South Face, then reverse the glacier approach back to camp.
runs: the standard north face route on the front

text: Start on the right side of the south face, above the East Nooksack Glacier, and front-point partway up the snow chute. Exit left onto a sloping ledge and change from crampons and boots to rock shoes; carrying the boots and tools up the rock makes for heavy packs.
runs: on the right side of the south face

text:
The whole route-finding problem is which glacier you end up on, and the answer is the east one. The rib above Price Lake has the Price Glacier on one side and the East Nooksack on the other. The Beckey route commits to the Price. This route commits to the East Nooksack. That single decision, made at the top of the rib, is the difference between a north-face ice couloir and a south-face rock climb, and once you are on the wrong glacier nothing further down the day will correct it.

The aspect settles it in fog, with no visibility at all. This route faces south. If the wall in front of you is in shade all morning and holds ice, you are under the north face and on the Beckey route's ground. If the wall catches the sun and is dry rock, you are where you meant to be.

Arrival: the south face rises directly above the glacier — there is no intervening basin, moraine or approach slope. You walk on ice until the ice ends at the wall. That directness is the marker; a wall you reach after scrambling up talus is not this one.

And the start is on the right. Having reached the foot of the face, the climb begins on its right side. A party that starts up the middle or the left of a twelve-pitch face on a rarely climbed tower has committed to unknown ground with a technical descent waiting for them.

Descent note that double-checks the start: the first-ascent party did not reverse this face. They descended the standard north-face route on the front of the tower, i.e. over the top and down the other side. If you are planning to rappel your line of ascent, you are planning something nobody has recorded.
runs: descended the standard north face route on the front

text: A short, fun 3-pitch 5.6-5.7 outing on Lexington Tower's north side, reached via the Concord-Lexington col above Liberty Bowl. The route climbs blocky, well-protected granite past an awkward leaning first-pitch crack to a finishing knife-edge ridge nicknamed 'the Stegosaur.' It was the original 1954 first-ascent line up the tower (Tim Kelley and Dick McGowan, July 5, 1954) and remains a good half-day objective away from the crowds on Liberty Bell and the Early Winters Spires.
runs: away from the crowds on liberty bell and

text: Crux of the route right off the ground: an awkward rightward-trending handcrack, easing above to a large belay block slung with tat.
runs: to a large belay block slung with tat

text: Cross the moat and start in the blocky line of face holds just left of the gully/chimney that bounds the left edge of the buttress. Most of the pitch is low fifth class on clean granite; a wide crack near the top holds the harder moves. The moat at the start can be awkward and changes through the season.
runs: in the blocky line of face holds just left of the

text: Trend up and right to the top of the lingering snow patch, aiming for the clean wall beneath a shallow left-facing corner. How much snow sits here varies a lot year to year, and in a big year it can bury this ground; belay at the base of the clean wall.
runs: up and right to the top of the

text: Follow flakes and cracks left onto a bright quartz dike, which gives about two pitches of continuous positive holds with only occasional gear. From a small ledge below the summit, a hidden snow patch and a steep final rock wall with an overhanging pull-up move lead to the top; an ice tool helps if that snow is still there.
runs: occasional gear from a small ledge below the summit

text:
The face is about fourteen hundred feet of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs above a glacier and it carries several routes with nothing marked. Do not identify by name; identify by feature.

First, place the central buttress. Stand back on the glacier and find the summit, then look at the buttress directly beneath it — that is the neighbouring route, and this line is not on it. This route takes the left margin of that buttress system, so you want to be off to the left of the plumb line from the summit.

Second, find the gully or chimney at the buttress's left edge. The start is in the blocky line of face holds just left of it. Blocky face holds, immediately left of a gully or chimney, at the left edge of the buttress: that is the whole identification at the ground. The first pitch is long, mostly low fifth class, with a wide crack near its end.

Third, and this is the confirmation higher up that nothing else on the face gives you: this route follows a distinctive yellow quartz dyke up the wall to avoid the dirtier rock either side of it. A yellow band running up the granite is not a subtle feature. If you never meet one, you are on a different climb.

Watch for an awkward bergschrund or moat where the glacier meets the rock.

Negative markers, and they matter because two of the neighbours are hard: if the summit is directly overhead from your belay and your second pitch is desperate face climbing wanting an aid move, you are on the central buttress line. And the face's original route and at least two others also exist here, so the honest rule is that anything without the yellow dyke above it is not this.

Descent is not the route reversed and not a rappel: take the east ridge from the top to an obvious col, then a snow finger back down toward the approach glacier and basin.
runs: in the blocky line of face holds just left of

text:
Whichever way you arrive, the glacier is the same and so is the identification, and this side has one advantage worth using: you come down toward the wall, which gives you the whole face in one view before you are under it. Take that view rather than sorting the routes out from the bergschrund.

From back on the glacier, find the summit and note the buttress directly under it — that is the neighbouring line and it is not this one. This route is on the left margin of the same buttress system.

The ground marker is a gully or chimney at the buttress's left edge, with the route starting in the blocky line of face holds just left of it. The confirmation above is a yellow quartz dyke, which the line follows deliberately to stay on clean rock and away from the dirtier granite either side. Yellow band, left margin, blocky start beside a chimney: those three together are the route.

Expect an awkward bergschrund or moat at the transition from ice to rock.

Negative markers. Directly under the summit with a very hard second pitch means the central buttress line. No yellow dyke anywhere above you means one of the other lines on this face, of which there are several and none is marked.

Second negative marker and it is not about climbing: the boundary clearing is a visible cut line across this ground. It is not a route and it is not a shortcut.

Descent is the east ridge to an obvious col and then a snow finger back to the glacier and basin.
runs: in the blocky line of face holds just left of
the east ridge to an obvious col and

text: The North Face of The Mole (Edward Peak, 7,280 ft) is an amazing alpine rock route offering 500 feet of easy, adventurous 5.7 climbing on the tallest of a quartet of granite spires at the northern fringe of the Enchantments, with unique views of the Icicle River valley.
runs: 500 feet of easy adventurous 5.7 climbing on

text: Follow the obvious large crack system, which splits into two variations around 60 meters, both rated 5.7. The climbing throughout both pitches is consistent and enjoyable with no stand-out crux. Mossy cracks lead up and to the left, then back right onto the summit. An easy sandy gully (or snow) leads to the base.
runs: up and to the left then back right

text: Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft) is 0.5 mile past milepost 162 on the south side of SR-20; vault toilet, ~20 parking spots, no potable water.
runs: mile past milepost 162 on the south side of

text: The base is the top of the notch between Concord Tower and Liberty Bell, reached by the gully — if you scrambled left out of the gully a couple of hundred feet below the notch onto a broad sloping bench, you are on Liberty Bell's west side and on a different mountain's route entirely. From the notch, the first pitch follows a crack system to a large ledge with some small trees growing on it; that ledge with trees is the confirmation you are on the North Face and not somewhere else on the tower. The second pitch is where this line parts from the standard route. From the tree ledge, head right toward a striking vertical crack and climb it until it gets harder, then traverse up and left across the face to a huge boulder or chockstone slung with tat. If you climbed straight up hollow, flaky rock to a short blank wall covered in huge huecos, you are on the standard North Face instead; going right after that hueco wall leads onto the Cave Route, not this variation. Expect severe rope drag on that long right-then-left pitch; extend everything.
runs: the top of the notch between concord tower and liberty bell
a crack system to a large ledge with some small trees

text: North Gardner Mountain (8,956 ft) is the highest point in Okanogan County and the 20th-highest peak on the Washington Bulger List (the state's 100 highest summits with 400+ ft of prominence). It sits within the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness on the east side of the Cascade Crest above the Methow Valley, joined by a high connecting ridge to 8,898 ft Gardner Mountain, 59 ft lower. The standard Southwest Slopes/South Ridge line is a long, remote scramble: roughly 10 miles of trail approach up Wolf Creek to Gardner Meadows, then off-trail travel through Wolf Creek Basin and a loose scree/snow bowl to the south ridge at Point 8,487, followed by a short final ridge walk to the true summit. Terrain is mostly Class 1-2 with a few short Class 3 steps; the crux for most parties is route-finding and about 1,400 ft of loose scree below Point 8,487, not technical climbing.
runs: on the east side of the cascade crest

text: From SR 20 in Winthrop, turn onto White Avenue just after the bridge over the Methow River; it becomes Twin Lakes Road. At 1.3 miles turn right onto Wolf Creek Road, follow it 2.9 miles, then turn left onto Wildflower Road, which becomes FS Road 5005 in about half a mile. Follow the signs to the Wolf Creek Trail at the road end, about 4 miles on.
runs: 1.3 miles turn right onto wolf creek road

text: Starting from the North Ridge Notch, climbers ascend a trough and over unprotected 5.6 slab to gain the ridge crest, then follow 2nd- and 3rd-class ramps and corners favoring the east (left) side of the crest. A short 5.0 downclimb bypasses the final gendarme before a sustained 5.4 pitch up the summit headwall (crux moves can be linked with the final pitch on a 70m rope) finishes at the true summit.
runs: unprotected 5.6 slab to gain the ridge crest

text: From the notch, climb a trough and an unprotected 5.6 slab traverse to the crest, then follow ramps and corners on the east (left) side of the crest. Downclimb a short 5.0 step off the last gendarme, cross the flat section of the ridge, and climb the 5.4 summit headwall to the top.
runs: ramps and corners on the east left side of the

text:
At the boulder field, bear right and north into the basin beneath the north ridge notch, rather than left toward the south buttress gully. That is the fork, and left versus right is the whole difference between two of this peak's routes.

The route's real base is the notch, and getting to it is itself a pitch: from the basin, A loose, runout 5.7 PG13 pitch gains the north ridge notch. Protection is marginal, one or two small cams and narrow-head-width pieces help, and this pitch should be treated as the technical and psychological crux of the approach, not of the ridge above it.

So the test is blunt: if the hardest, scariest thing you have done is the pitch that got you to the notch, you are on the right route. If you got to a notch by walking, you are somewhere else.

Arrival: a notch, a gap on the crest with the ridge running above it. Everything above is the North Ridge.

The northern alternative, which arrives at the same notch from the other side: from Rainy Pass, follow the Pacific Crest Trail into the Porcupine Creek drainage, then climb two or three short pitches of low fifth class to gain the North Ridge Notch from that side. That is a legitimate option for parties camping near Rainy Pass, and it adds significant approach time. Two or three easy pitches versus one hard runout one is how you tell which side you came up.

Descent does not reverse the approach pitch all the way: from the summit, reverse the North Ridge with several short rappels through the steeper fifth-class steps, then one longer rappel back into the North Ridge Notch. From the notch, descend via the standard South Buttress and West Ridge line, downclimbing to the first set of bolted chain rappel anchors and continuing down the same four-rappel West Ridge sequence, a single 60 m rope sufficient for each, before the final scramble through the scree bowl and boulder field back to the meadow and creek crossing.
runs: short pitches of low fifth class to gain the north ridge notch

text: Via McAllister Camp (~6 mi in) and the climbers' trail up the ridge between McAllister and Thunder Creeks to the bivy at the toe of the Borealis Glacier, then around the glacial lake and across a short stretch of glacier to the foot of the North Ridge. The usual descent is the East Ridge to Lucky Pass (7,200 ft) and down the Borealis Glacier.
runs: climbers trail up the ridge between mcallister and thunder creeks

text: Follow the Thunder Creek Trail about 6 miles to McAllister Camp, then the climbers' trail up the ridge between McAllister and Thunder Creeks to a bivy near 6,000 ft at the Borealis Glacier's toe. Rather than heading for Lucky Pass, circle the glacial lake at the terminus and cross a short stretch of glacier to the foot of the North Ridge, then climb about 1,000 ft of loose blocks, towers and banded low-fifth rock to the summit.
runs: climbers trail up the ridge between mcallister and thunder creeks

text: Same Thunder Creek Trailhead approach as the East Slope route (Colonial Creek Campground on SR 20, about 6 miles up the Thunder Creek Trail to McAllister Camp, then the climbers' trail up the ridge between McAllister and Thunder Creeks to a bivy at ~6,000 ft near the toe of the Borealis Glacier) — the North Ridge is reached by traversing around the lake instead of climbing the glacier from camp.
runs: climbers trail up the ridge between mcallister and thunder creeks

text: Exposed ridge climb combining three to four pitches of fourth-class scrambling with a final 40-foot 5.5 pitch to a short tower. Easily completed as a half-day climb from Boston Basin campsites.
runs: as a half day climb from boston basin

text: Approach as for Forbidden Peak and camp at lower (5,300 ft) or upper (6,400 ft) bivy sites. From camp, navigate toward Forbidden Gully or Cat Scratch Gullies and traverse toward the notch to the right of the North Ridge. Make three to four fourth-class pitches to tower base, then climb the crux 40-foot 5.5 pitch to the tower top. For descent, make one 40-foot rappel and reverse the ridge climb.
runs: traverse toward the notch to the right of the north ridge

text: Very light rack. The route is 2-3 pitches of nearly level ridge that's typically simul-climbed or short-roped, then a single steeper crux step (published descriptions call it 4th class, ~50-60ft; others describe it as up to 5.5) leading to the top of a short tower, where the route ends. A small set of cams from finger-size to roughly 2in plus a handful of nuts is enough to protect the crux step and build gear anchors — there is no fixed gear or anchors on-route apart from rappel slings waiting at the descent notch.
runs: there is no fixed gear or anchors on
